q: The boxes show a reaction mixture of A<sub>2</sub> and B<sub>2</sub> molecules before and after the reaction. Which balanced equation, with the smallest whole-number coefficients, represents the reaction?
h: Molecules that appear unchanged in both boxes did not react. Count only what was used up and what was made, then reduce.
w: Before: 5 A2 and 3 B2. After: 4 A2B plus 1 A2 and 1 B2 left over. So 4 A2 + 2 B2 made 4 A2B, which reduces to 2 A2 + B2 → 2 A2B. Leftover molecules are not part of the equation, and A2 + B2 → A2B is not balanced for A.
x: Leftover A₂ and B₂ molecules did not react, so they do not belong in the equation.
This is not balanced. Count the A atoms on each side.
These coefficients can still be divided by a common factor.

q: Nitrogen monoxide reacts with chlorine as shown. The Before box shows the starting mixture. Which box (I–IV) shows the contents after the reaction goes to completion?
h: Find the limiting reactant from the 2 : 1 mole ratio. At completion it is gone, and every atom from the Before box must still be present.
w: 6 NO need only 3 Cl2, and 5 Cl2 are present, so NO is limiting. 6 NO + 3 Cl2 → 6 NOCl, leaving 2 Cl2: box III. Box I still has both reactants, so the reaction is not complete. Box II shows lone Cl atoms, but leftover chlorine stays as Cl2. Box IV has 16 Cl atoms but only 10 were present.
x: This box still contains both NO and Cl₂, so the reaction has not gone to completion.
Leftover chlorine stays as Cl₂ molecules. It does not split into separate atoms.
Count the Cl atoms. This box has more chlorine than the Before box.

q: Hydrogen sulfide burns as shown. The box shows a mixture of H<sub>2</sub>S and O<sub>2</sub>. What would have to be added to the box so that both reactants are completely used up with nothing left over?
h: Count each reactant. Find how much of each the other one needs using the 2 : 3 ratio, and see which one is short.
w: The box holds 4 H2S and 9 O2. 4 H2S need only 6 O2, so O2 is in excess. 9 O2 need 9 × 2/3 = 6 H2S, so 2 more H2S molecules must be added. 6 is the total H2S needed, not the number to add, and 5 assumes a 1 : 1 ratio.
x: Six is the total number of H₂S molecules needed. Some are already in the box.
This assumes H₂S and O₂ react 1 to 1. Use the coefficients 2 and 3.
O₂ is already in excess here. Adding more of it leaves even more unused.

q: Potassium chlorate decomposes on heating as shown. What mass of O<sub>2</sub> forms when 5.00 g of KClO<sub>3</sub> decomposes completely?
h: Grams of KClO<sub>3</sub> → moles of KClO<sub>3</sub> → moles of O<sub>2</sub> (use the 2 : 3 ratio) → grams of O<sub>2</sub>.
w: 5.00 g / 122.55 g mol−1 = 0.04080 mol KClO3. × (3 mol O2 / 2 mol KClO3) = 0.06120 mol O2. × 32.00 g mol−1 = 1.96 g. 1.31 g uses a 1 : 1 ratio, 0.870 g turns the ratio upside down, and 3.92 g uses 3 mol O2 for every mole of KClO3.
x: This uses a 1 to 1 mole ratio. The equation shows 3 O₂ for every 2 KClO₃.
This turns the mole ratio upside down. More moles of O₂ form than moles of KClO₃ used.
This takes 3 mol O₂ from each mole of KClO₃. The coefficients give 3 O₂ per 2 KClO₃.

q: Yeast ferments glucose to ethanol as shown. A batch starting with 100.0 g of glucose yields 40.0 g of ethanol. What is the percent yield?
h: First find the theoretical yield of ethanol in grams from the glucose. Percent yield = actual/theoretical × 100.
w: 100.0 g / 180.16 g mol−1 = 0.5551 mol glucose → 1.110 mol ethanol × 46.07 g mol−1 = 51.14 g (theoretical). Percent yield = 40.0/51.14 × 100 = 78.2%. 40.0% compares masses of different substances, 156% uses a 1 : 1 ratio, and 128% divides theoretical by actual.
x: This compares grams of ethanol with grams of glucose directly. Find the theoretical yield of ethanol first.
A yield above 100% is a warning sign. Check the mole ratio of ethanol to glucose.
This divides the theoretical yield by the actual yield. The actual yield goes on top.

q: In a series of experiments, 2.00 g of zinc is heated with different masses of sulfur, and the mass of ZnS formed is measured (graph). Zn + S → ZnS. In the experiment at point B, which reactant is limiting, and what is left over?
c: Zn is limiting, and about 0.52 g of S is left
S is limiting, and about 0.52 g of Zn is left
Zn is limiting, and about 1.50 g of S is left
Neither, both reactants are used up exactly
h: On the rising part of the graph, adding more S makes more ZnS. On the flat part, adding S makes no more product. Where does the line level off?
w: The mass of ZnS stops rising at about 0.98 g of S (2.00 g Zn / 65.38 g mol−1 = 0.0306 mol needs 0.0306 mol × 32.06 = 0.98 g S). At point B, 1.50 g of S was added, so Zn is limiting and about 0.52 g of S is left (1.50 − 0.98). S is the limiting reactant only on the rising part, such as point A.
x: On the flat part adding more sulfur makes no more ZnS, so sulfur is not what limits the product there.
Only part of the sulfur at point B reacts. Find where the graph levels off.
At point B more sulfur was added than the zinc can use. The exact match is where the graph levels off.

q: A solution of a metal ion M<sup>n+</sup> and a NaOH solution, both 0.100 M, are mixed in different proportions. The total volume is always 12.0 mL. The precipitate M(OH)<sub>n</sub> is collected and weighed (graph). What is the value of n?

x.label: Volume of 0.100 M NaOH (mL); the rest is 0.100 M M<sup>n+</sup>

h: The most precipitate forms when the two ions are mixed in exactly the ratio of the formula. Read the volumes of the two solutions at the peak.
w: The peak is at 9.0 mL of NaOH, which leaves 3.0 mL of the Mn+ solution. Both are 0.100 M, so the mole ratio OH− : Mn+ = 9.0 : 3.0 = 3 : 1. The formula is M(OH)3, so n = 3. A ratio of 1 or 2 would put the peak at 6.0 mL or 8.0 mL of NaOH.
x: A 1 to 1 ratio would put the peak at 6 mL of each solution. Read where this peak is.
A 2 to 1 ratio would put the peak at 8 mL of NaOH. Read the peak on the graph again.
A 4 to 1 ratio would put the peak at 9.6 mL of NaOH. Read the peak on the graph again.

q: Ammonia gas passed over hot copper(II) oxide reduces it to copper metal (skeleton equation below). When the equation is balanced with the smallest whole-number coefficients, what is the coefficient of CuO?
h: Start with N: N<sub>2</sub> needs two NH<sub>3</sub>. Then balance H with water, O with CuO, and Cu last.
w: N2 needs 2 NH3, whose 6 H make 3 H2O. Three O atoms require 3 CuO, which give 3 Cu: 2 NH3 + 3 CuO → 3 Cu + N2 + 3 H2O. Check: N 2 = 2, H 6 = 6, Cu 3 = 3, O 3 = 3.
x: Two is the coefficient of NH₃. Balance H with water and then match the O atoms with CuO.
With one CuO there is only one O atom, but the H atoms from ammonia need more water than that.
These are not the smallest whole numbers. Check whether the whole set can be halved.

q: Acetone, drawn below, burns completely in oxygen to give CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O. How many moles of O<sub>2</sub> are needed to burn 0.250 mol of acetone?
h: Read the formula from the drawing and write the balanced combustion equation. Don't forget the oxygen atom already in acetone.
w: Acetone is C3H6O: C3H6O + 4 O2 → 3 CO2 + 3 H2O (O: 1 + 8 = 6 + 3). 0.250 mol × 4 = 1.00 mol O2. 1.13 mol ignores the O atom in acetone, and 0.750 mol is the amount of CO2 (or H2O) formed.
x: This leaves out the oxygen atom that acetone already contains. Count it when balancing O.
This is the amount of CO₂ produced, not the O₂ consumed.
This divides by the coefficient instead of multiplying. More O₂ is needed than acetone.

q: 5.00 g of iron and 8.00 g of chlorine react as shown until one reactant is used up. What mass of the excess reactant remains?
h: Convert both masses to moles. Find which one runs out first using the 2 : 3 ratio, then find how much of the other one reacts.
w: Fe: 5.00/55.85 = 0.0895 mol. Cl2: 8.00/70.90 = 0.1128 mol. All the Fe would need 0.134 mol Cl2, more than is present, so Cl2 is limiting. Fe used = 0.1128 × 2/3 = 0.0752 mol = 4.20 g, so 0.80 g of Fe remains. 4.20 g is the iron that reacts, and 3.00 g of Cl2 assumes the smaller mass runs out.
x: This treats iron as limiting. Check whether there is enough Cl₂ for all of the iron.
Subtracting the masses does not find the limiting reactant. Compare moles using the coefficients.
This is the mass of iron that reacts. The question asks what is left.

q:
The box shows a mixture of P4 molecules (four P atoms each) and Cl2 molecules that react as shown until one reactant is used up. Which statements are true?
I. Cl2 is the limiting reactant.
II. The total number of molecules in the box is the same after the reaction.
III. The total mass of the box contents is the same after the reaction.
h: Count the molecules of each reactant and use the 1 : 6 ratio. Then count the molecules after the reaction and think about what happens to atoms.
w: The box has 2 P4 and 6 Cl2. Two P4 would need 12 Cl2, so I is true: Cl2 runs out. 6 Cl2 + 1 P4 → 4 PCl3, leaving 1 P4, so there are 5 molecules after versus 8 before, and II is false. III is true because atoms are conserved, so mass is conserved. The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement III is also true. Every atom is still in the box, so the mass cannot change.
Statement II is false. Count the molecules before and after.
Statement I is true. Two P₄ molecules would need twelve Cl₂ molecules.

q:
A student burns a strip of magnesium in a crucible open to the air, so O2 is always in excess. Which statements are true?
I. Using more O2 would increase the theoretical yield of MgO.
II. Using a longer strip of Mg would increase the theoretical yield of MgO.
III. If some MgO smoke escapes, the percent yield is lowered.
h: The theoretical yield depends only on the amount of the limiting reactant. The percent yield compares what is collected with that amount.
w: Mg is the limiting reactant. I is false: more of an excess reactant does not change the theoretical yield. II is true: more Mg means more MgO can form. III is true: lost product lowers the actual yield, so the percent yield drops (the theoretical yield is unchanged). The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement I is false. O₂ is already in excess, so adding more cannot raise the theoretical yield.
Statement III is also true. Product that escapes is not weighed, so the actual yield falls.
Statement I is false. Extra excess reactant does not change how much product can form.

q:
Each fuel below burns completely to CO2 and H2O. Rank them by the mass of CO2 produced per gram of fuel burned, from least to most.
I. methane, CH4
II. ethane, C2H6
III. propane, C3H8
h: Every C atom in the fuel ends up in one CO<sub>2</sub>. Compare the mass fraction of carbon in each fuel.
w: Grams of CO2 per gram = (number of C × 44.01)/molar mass. CH4: 44.01/16.04 = 2.74. C2H6: 88.02/30.07 = 2.93. C3H8: 132.03/44.10 = 2.99. So I < II < III: the larger the fuel, the higher its fraction of carbon.
x: This is the reverse. Methane has the most hydrogen per carbon, so it has the lowest fraction of carbon.
Ethane has a higher fraction of carbon than methane, so it gives more CO₂ per gram.
Propane has a higher fraction of carbon than ethane. Work out grams of CO₂ per gram for each.

q: A sample of cobalt(II) chloride hydrate, CoCl<sub>2</sub>·nH<sub>2</sub>O, is heated in a crucible until all the water is driven off. The data are shown. What is n? (CoCl<sub>2</sub>: 129.83 g mol<sup>−1</sup>; H<sub>2</sub>O: 18.02 g mol<sup>−1</sup>)
h: Find the mass of the hydrate, the anhydrous residue and the water lost. Convert the water and the CoCl<sub>2</sub> to moles and take their ratio.
w: Hydrate = 20.832 − 18.452 = 2.380 g. CoCl2 = 19.752 − 18.452 = 1.300 g, which is 0.01001 mol. Water lost = 2.380 − 1.300 = 1.080 g, which is 0.05993 mol. n = 0.05993/0.01001 = 5.99, so n = 6. 13 treats the whole hydrate mass as water, and 1 compares grams instead of moles.
x: This treats the whole hydrate mass as water. Subtract the residue to get the water lost.
This compares the masses of water and CoCl₂ directly. Convert both to moles first.
Check the subtraction. The water lost is the hydrate mass minus the residue mass.

q: A mixture of 2.00 mol of Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> and 5.40 mol of carbon reacts as shown. What is the theoretical yield of iron?
h: Find how much Fe each reactant could make on its own. The smaller amount is the theoretical yield.
w: From Fe2O3: 2.00 × 2 = 4.00 mol Fe. From C: 5.40 × 2/3 = 3.60 mol Fe. Carbon is limiting, so the theoretical yield is 3.60 mol. 4.00 mol would need 6.00 mol C, which is not available.
x: This is what Fe₂O₃ alone could make, but there is not enough carbon for all of it.
This uses a 1 to 1 ratio of C to Fe. The coefficients are 3 and 2.
This turns the C to Fe ratio upside down. Three C atoms give two Fe atoms.

q: Nitrogen reacts with fluorine as shown. Which box (I–IV) contains N<sub>2</sub> and F<sub>2</sub> in exactly the right ratio for both to be used up completely?
h: The coefficients say one N<sub>2</sub> molecule for every three F<sub>2</sub> molecules.
w: Box II has 2 N2 and 6 F2, a 1 : 3 ratio, so it makes 4 NF3 with nothing left: box II. Box I (1 : 1) leaves N2 over, box III (3 : 1) has the ratio upside down, and box IV (1 : 6) leaves F2 over.
x: Equal numbers of molecules do not match a 1 to 3 ratio. N₂ would be left over.
This box has the ratio upside down, with more N₂ than F₂.
One N₂ uses only three F₂, so F₂ would be left over.

q: Calcium carbide is made in two steps, shown below. What maximum mass of CaC<sub>2</sub> can be made from 50.0 g of CaCO<sub>3</sub> if carbon is in excess? (CaCO<sub>3</sub>: 100.09 g mol<sup>−1</sup>; CaC<sub>2</sub>: 64.10 g mol<sup>−1</sup>)
h: Follow the calcium: one CaCO<sub>3</sub> gives one CaO, which gives one CaC<sub>2</sub>. The coefficient of carbon does not matter here.
w: 50.0 g / 100.09 g mol−1 = 0.4996 mol CaCO3 → 0.4996 mol CaO → 0.4996 mol CaC2. Mass = 0.4996 × 64.10 = 32.0 g. 10.7 g and 96.1 g wrongly bring in the coefficient 3 on carbon, and 64.1 g is the mass of one full mole.
x: This divides by the 3 on carbon. Carbon is in excess, so it does not set the ratio of CaC₂ to CaCO₃.
This multiplies by the 3 on carbon. Each CaO gives one CaC₂.
This is the mass of one mole of CaC₂. Only about half a mole of CaCO₃ is used.

q: Chlorine and fluorine react to form chlorine trifluoride. The boxes show the mixture before the reaction and after it has stopped. What is the percent yield of ClF<sub>3</sub>?
h: Work out how many ClF<sub>3</sub> molecules could form if the reaction went to completion, then compare with how many did form.
w: 3 Cl2 and 9 F2 are in the exact 1 : 3 ratio, so 6 ClF3 could form. Only 4 formed, with 1 Cl2 and 3 F2 left. Percent yield = 4/6 × 100 = 66.7%. 44.4% divides by the 9 F2, 133% divides by the 3 Cl2, and 50.0% is the share of molecules in the After box that are ClF3.
x: This divides by the number of F₂ molecules. Compare with the most ClF₃ that could form.
A yield over 100% is impossible. Each Cl₂ can make two ClF₃.
This is the fraction of molecules after the reaction that are product, not the percent yield.

q: Which statement correctly describes the balanced equation for the combustion of ethane?
c: 2 mol of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> react with 7 mol of O<sub>2</sub>.
2 g of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> react with 7 g of O<sub>2</sub>.
The products weigh more than the reactants, since 10 mol form from 9 mol.
2 molecules of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> react with 7 atoms of oxygen.
h: Coefficients count particles (molecules or moles), not grams.
w: Coefficients give the ratio of molecules or moles, so 2 mol of C2H6 react with 7 mol of O2. They are not mass ratios. Mass is always conserved even though the number of moles changes (9 → 10). The 7 counts O2 molecules, which is 14 O atoms.
x: Coefficients count moles or molecules, not grams. The two gases have different molar masses.
Mass is conserved in every reaction. Moles of molecules are not.
The coefficient 7 counts O₂ molecules, and each one has two O atoms.

q: Substances A and B react to form a single product, C. In each trial in the table the reaction goes until one reactant is used up. Which equation fits the data?
h: In trial 1, B is plentiful, so A must run out. In trial 2, A is plentiful, so B must run out. Each tells you one coefficient.
w: Trial 1: if A limits, 1.00 mol A gives 0.500 mol C, so 2 A per C. Trial 2: if B limits, 1.50 mol B gives 0.500 mol C, so 3 B per C. Trial 3 checks it: 2.00 mol A and 3.00 mol B are used up exactly and give 1.00 mol C. The equation is 2 A + 3 B → C. 2 A + 10 B → C assumes all of B reacts in trial 1, but then trial 2 could make only 0.15 mol C.
x: These coefficients are swapped. In trial 2, find how many moles of B make 0.500 mol C.
This assumes all 5.00 mol of B reacts in trial 1. Test it on trial 2, where it predicts far less C.
With a 1 to 1 to 1 ratio, trial 1 would give 1.00 mol C. Compare that with the table.
